claims: A retail price index measures changes in the cost of a representative consumer basket relative to a base period.
A simple fixed-basket price index equals current basket cost divided by base basket cost, multiplied by 100.
Inflation between two index periods is the index increase divided by the earlier index, multiplied by 100.
Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level, not simply a rise in one product price.
Demand-pull, cost-push and monetary accounts identify different causal mechanisms that can overlap rather than necessarily exclusive events.
Real income is income adjusted for the price level, indicating purchasing power.
General price increases reduce the purchasing power of unchanged money income or balances.
Inflation can affect borrowers, lenders, firms and households differently depending on expectations, income adjustments, interest and contracts.
Demand-pull inflation is sustained general price pressure arising when aggregate demand grows beyond the economy’s ability to expand real output sufficiently.
Extra demand is more likely to raise prices strongly where productive capacity is constrained than where output can readily expand.
Cost-push inflation is sustained general price pressure associated with rising production costs or adverse supply conditions.
Higher imported-input costs can create cost pressure, though pass-through, demand and other conditions affect the general-price result.
Monetary inflation refers to price pressure associated with monetary expansion supporting nominal spending faster than real output can respond.
An increased money supply is not by itself proof of immediate inflation because money demand, spending behaviour and productive capacity also matter.

CU-6145-7.1:
A retail price index measures changes in the cost of a representative consumer basket relative to a base period. The basket gives a consistent set of goods and services for comparison. A base index of 100 is a reference, not a money amount or a claim that every product costs N$100. Prices can be combined using their importance in the basket rather than assuming a small purchase and a large household expense have equal weight. A fixed-quantity basket provides a simple way to incorporate those weights through quantities.

In an invented basket, four food packs cost N$25 each and two transport services N$50 each in the base period, giving N$200 total. In the later period the same quantities cost N$30 and N$60, giving N$240. The index is 240 divided by 200 times 100 = 120. The basket is 20 percent more expensive than in the base period. The quantities are held constant so the comparison measures prices rather than more consumption. These are teaching items, not official Namibia index weights or actual household statistics. A representative index can be useful while individual households experience different price changes because their spending patterns differ.

An index level and an inflation rate are different measures. Index 120 means a 20 percent increase relative to base 100. If the next index is 126, inflation from 120 to 126 is six divided by 120 times 100 = 5 percent, not 6 percent and not 26 percent. Six is the index-point rise, 5 percent the change relative to the preceding period, and 26 percent the cumulative change from base 100. State which comparison is requested before choosing a denominator.

A falling inflation rate does not necessarily mean prices fall. A move from 10 percent annual inflation to 5 percent means the general level is still rising, but more slowly. A falling general level is a different situation. Nor does one product’s price rise establish the general trend. A basket combines changes across items, some of which may fall while others rise. Keep the observation, measure and time period clear. A comparison of two index numbers can quantify the change, but it does not identify whether demand, cost or monetary conditions caused it. Those mechanisms require separate evidence from the case.

The base-period comparison can be checked by rebuilding the basket total from its components before dividing. If a component price is omitted, the index no longer describes the stated basket. If the quantity changes, the comparison mixes spending and prices. These checks protect the meaning of the result rather than merely repeat a percentage calculation. The learner should be able to explain why the basket costs differ and which features were deliberately kept constant.

Real income is income adjusted for the price level. An unchanged monetary income buys less when the relevant basket becomes more expensive. A household receiving N$5,000 with an index moving from 100 to 125 has later real income of N$5,000 divided by 125 times 100 = N$4,000 at base prices. The money amount is unchanged, while purchasing power is 20 percent below its original N$5,000 base-price value. A 25 percent price increase does not imply an exact 25 percent purchasing-power fall; the index ratio gives the correct relationship.

If money income also changes, deflate the new amount before comparing. Disposable income is different: taxes and deductions determine the funds available, while the price adjustment determines their buying power. Inflation may also reduce the real value of unchanged balances unless interest or other changes offset it. Do not assume a household’s own basket exactly matches the representative index. The supplied exercise defines the comparison basis. Explain the result as purchasing power for that basis rather than inventing an identical loss for each resident.

Inflation can affect groups differently. A borrower with a fixed nominal debt may benefit from an unexpected fall in its real burden, while a lender may receive repayment with less purchasing power. The actual effect depends on interest, income changes and whether inflation was expected when terms were agreed. The borrower still needs the cash to make payments; a smaller real debt is not proof of easier monthly affordability. Firms can face uncertain costs and selling conditions, making planning harder, while the effect on profit depends on both receipts and complete costs.

An explanation should therefore name the affected person, the contract or income condition and the mechanism. Avoid saying inflation helps all borrowers or harms all firms identically. The cause also matters to the policy response: demand growing beyond capacity differs from an input-cost shock even if both raise the general level. This links the measurement to the mechanisms in the next unit and economic policy in 6.2. A sustained trend, a one-off relative-price change and an individual experience should be kept distinct so the learner can interpret the data without supplying their own unsupported facts.
CU-6145-7.1.2:
Demand-pull inflation is sustained general price pressure when aggregate demand grows beyond the economy’s ability to expand real output sufficiently. Demand concerns total spending pressure, not just popularity of one shop’s product. If many buyers seek more output while capacity and inputs are limited, firms may be unable to meet the extra demand mainly by producing more. Prices can then respond strongly. Where resources are unused and available to the relevant activities, additional demand may instead support a larger real output response with less price pressure.

An invented economy experiencing broad growth in consumption, investment and public purchases near capacity illustrates the mechanism. The explanation should identify spending pressure and constrained supply rather than merely quote rising prices. A policy restraining demand may reduce that pressure but can also affect output and jobs, so evaluation considers unused resources and priorities. The presence of a capacity bottleneck does not mean every sector is equally constrained. Some workers or equipment can be unused while a particular input is scarce. State the relevant evidence before claiming an economy-wide result. Demand-pull is a causal account for the general trend, not a label assigned automatically to each individual price rise. To assess a supplied case, ask whether the information describes broad spending growth relative to feasible real production and whether the pressure persists, rather than an isolated surge in one product’s demand. A useful contrast holds supply response clear: extra spending when suitable capacity is available can increase output, whereas the same spending pressure with a binding bottleneck may produce more price adjustment. This is a conditional mechanism, not a precise forecast of the inflation rate from a spending figure alone.

Cost-push inflation is sustained general price pressure associated with rising production costs or adverse supply conditions. Higher important input costs can affect many firms, making the same output more costly to produce. Firms may seek higher prices, reduce output or accept lower margins, depending on demand and circumstances. An isolated cost increase at a small producer does not establish a sustained general rise. Explain how the shock is broad enough and transmitted through the economy rather than assume a single expense determines the whole price index.

Imported fuel or materials can be a source of pressure in an invented case. If a foreign-currency input price is unchanged but the domestic currency weakens against that currency, more domestic money is needed for the same purchase. That increases the importer’s domestic cost, rather than lowering it. How much reaches selling prices depends on competition, contracts and buyers’ responses. This corrects a direction error without predicting a uniform outcome. Similarly, a general disruption to essential supply can raise costs and constrain output, while a demand-only explanation would miss the initial cause. Policy should address the actual pressure where feasible, while recognising that using resources elsewhere has an opportunity cost. This mechanism can overlap with demand conditions: strong spending may make pass-through easier, while weak demand can limit it. The labels identify channels rather than mutually exclusive boxes into which every event must fit. Distinguish a change in the cost level from a sustained process. A single input shock may raise some prices once, while continuing shocks or wider adjustments can sustain the general trend. The supplied period and evidence determine what can be claimed. Do not invent repeated shocks merely to convert an isolated example into a sustained national account.

Monetary inflation refers to price pressure associated with monetary expansion that supports nominal spending faster than real output can respond. The mechanism links money and credit conditions to spending and then to prices. It is not simply the existence of a larger money number. People may choose to hold more balances, spending behaviour may change and unused capacity may permit more real output. Those conditions affect whether expansion translates into immediate general price pressure.

In an invented case with expanding money and credit, rising broad spending and constrained production, the evidence can support a monetary contribution. The explanation should carry each stage rather than infer the result from the first fact alone. It can also overlap with demand-pull: the increased financing may support the demand pressure. Cost shocks can operate at the same time, so a careful answer identifies the information supporting each channel. A policy response depends on the actual cause, institutions and trade-offs rather than a slogan that money growth inevitably causes the same inflation everywhere. This links the type to monetary policy in 6.2 and banking in 2.3. For a comparison question, distinguish the initial change—spending pressure, cost/supply pressure or monetary conditions—while recognising how the channels interact. The shared outcome is a sustained rise in the general level, whose magnitude and consequences need further evidence. The three accounts should therefore be compared through the initial change and transmission mechanism. They are not three different measures of the price index. Measurement tells us what happened to the basket; causal analysis explains why, using separate supporting facts.

cards: Define a retail price index.
A measure of changes in the cost of a representative consumer basket relative to a base period.
Definition: basket cost change 1; qualifier: representative basket/base comparison 1.
Calculate the simple fixed-basket index when base cost is N$200 and current cost N$240, with base index 100.
Formula: current/base cost ×100. Working: 240/200 ×100 =120. Answer: index 120.
Formula/working shown for learning; answer index 120 earns the single result mark, with no currency unit.
Explain the change from price index 120 to 126.

The rise is six index points but 5 percent relative to 120. The basket is 5 percent more expensive than in the earlier period;126 also means 26 percent above base 100. These comparisons use different reference periods.
Relationship: index level versus rate 1; evidence: six/120 ×100=5 1; explanation: prior-period/base distinction 2.
Explain why holding basket quantities constant helps a simple price-index comparison.
It keeps the goods-and-services amounts comparable (1), so cost change reflects their prices rather than a larger quantity purchased (1).
Context: fixed basket; reasoning: common quantities 1; result: price effect isolated 1.
Identify the inflation account beginning with broad spending pressure exceeding real supply response.
Demand-pull (1).
Characteristic: demand relative to capacity, 1.
Explain the difference between demand-pull and cost-push accounts of inflation.
Demand-pull begins with broad demand outrunning output response (1), whereas cost-push begins with production-cost or adverse supply pressure (1).
Difference/distinguishing test: initial demand versus cost/supply change, 1 each.
Explain why a rise in one small shop’s price is insufficient evidence of general inflation.
Inflation concerns a sustained general price-level increase (1), so an isolated product or seller change does not establish the broader trend (1).
Context: shop price; reasoning: general/sustained measure 1; result: isolated evidence insufficient 1.
Define real income.
Income adjusted for the price level, indicating purchasing power.
Meaning: price-adjusted income 1; qualifier: buying power 1.
Explain how a general price increase affects an unchanged nominal household income.
Initial change: the same basket costs more (1); the household can buy less with unchanged money income, reducing real purchasing power (1).
Initial change 1; mechanism/effect for household: higher prices lower real resources 1.
Explain why inflation need not benefit every borrower equally.
Contract interest and income changes differ (1), so a lower real value of fixed debt does not guarantee easier cash repayments or a net gain (1).
Context: borrower comparison; reasoning: terms/income 1; result: conditional outcome 1.
Define demand-pull inflation.
Sustained general price pressure when aggregate demand grows beyond the economy’s ability to expand real output sufficiently.
Definition: general price pressure 1; qualifier: demand relative to capacity 1.
Define cost-push inflation.
Sustained general price pressure associated with rising production costs or adverse supply conditions.
Meaning: general price pressure 1; qualifier: cost/supply cause 1.
Define monetary inflation as a causal account.
Price pressure associated with monetary expansion supporting nominal spending faster than real output can respond.
Definition: monetary/spending pressure 1; qualifier: relative real response condition 1.
performance: An invented fixed consumer basket costs N$400 in base period A, N$440 in B and N$462 in C. Quantities and quality are unchanged. A household’s money income stays N$8,000. The case supplies no information about the causes of the price change. (a) Describe three price comparisons (6). (b) Examine what can be concluded about inflation and purchasing power (7). (c) Suggest how the evidence should guide further analysis (7).

(a) Base index is 100. B is 110, a 10 percent rise from A. C is 115.5, a 5 percent rise from B and 15.5 percent from A. (b) The basket becomes more expensive in both periods while the rate slows. The unchanged money income has lower purchasing power; at C, base-price income is 8000/1.155, about N$6,926.41. The index does not identify demand, cost or monetary cause or each household’s exact experience. (c) Check representative weights and period comparability, then seek evidence on spending, costs, supply and monetary conditions before assigning a cause. A slowing rate is not falling prices. The judgement should use the measured result while keeping causal and distributional claims conditional.

Context: basket. Parts/allocation: (a) base, B and C comparisons 2 each =6. (b) continuing rise/slowing rate 2, real-income evidence 3, causal/household limits 2 =7. (c) measurement checks 2, causal evidence 3, supported judgement 2 =7. Mechanism: unchanged income buys a smaller basket as its cost rises.

(a) Define inflation (2). (b) Define retail price index (2). (c) Explain index points versus percentage change (2). (d) Explain why lower positive inflation need not mean lower prices (2). (e) Explain one cost-push channel (2). (f) Explain one demand-pull condition (2). (g) Explain why money expansion alone is insufficient evidence of immediate inflation (2). (h) Explain why real income differs from disposable income (2).

(a) Sustained rise in general prices. (b) Representative basket cost relative to base. (c) Points are the arithmetic difference; percent divides by the earlier index. (d) Prices still rise at a slower rate. (e) An important input-cost increase may pass through to broad prices. (f) Demand grows faster than real output can expand. (g) Money demand, spending and output response also matter. (h) Real adjusts prices, disposable adjusts taxes/deductions.

Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2. (a) sustained + general; (b) basket + base; (c) difference + denominator; (d) positive level growth + slower rate; (e) input + pass-through; (f) demand + capacity; (g) monetary fact + transmission conditions; (h) two distinct adjustments.

In an invented economy, imported essential inputs become more costly in domestic currency, broad production is disrupted and household nominal pay is unchanged. Demand data are absent. (a) Define cost-push inflation (2). (b) Explain two distinctions needed to interpret the case (4). (c) Explain how the shock may affect firms and households (7). (d) Discuss whether it is enough to prescribe demand restraint without further evidence (7).

(a) General price pressure from rising costs or adverse supply. (b) Higher input costs differ from initial demand growth. Unchanged money income differs from unchanged purchasing power when prices move. (c) Firms face higher production requirements or costs, and may adjust prices, margins or output. Pass-through can reduce household purchasing power if the relevant general level rises. Results differ by costs, contracts and spending patterns; no exact inflation or profit figure is supplied. (d) Restraining demand could limit price pressure where spending contributes, but does not directly repair the supply disruption and may reduce output further. Seek evidence on demand, capacity and the shock’s persistence. The judgement should match the response to the cause and constraints rather than infer one policy from a price rise alone.

Context: imported shock. Parts/allocation: (a) general price 1, cost/supply cause 1. (b) cause and income distinctions 2 each=4. (c) firm mechanism 3, household mechanism 2, pass-through/data limits 2=7. (d) demand case 2, supply/output limit 2, conditional evidence judgement 3=7. Mechanism: imported costs affect production and possible prices; judgement matches response to evidenced cause.
Evaluate whether an invented adviser should claim that inflation benefits borrowers solely because fixed nominal debts lose real value, when income and interest terms are unknown (9).

For: unexpected inflation can reduce the purchasing power of the repayment on a fixed nominal debt, potentially favouring the borrower relative to the lender. Against: interest may reflect expected inflation, terms may change and the borrower’s income may fail to keep up with living costs. Cash affordability can worsen despite the lower real debt. Judgement: examine contract, expectations and income before assigning a net gain. The condition for the simple borrower benefit is an unchanged nominal obligation and a relevant purchasing-power comparison; it is not proof of easier payments for every borrower.
Argument for: fixed-debt real-value mechanism, up to 4. Argument against: terms/expectations/income and cash limits, up to 4. Judgement: distinct contract/affordability condition,1. Total 9.
judgements: Original basket and index data; no current national statistics implied. Index rates use earlier index, and exact real-income ratios replace percentage subtraction.
Monetary, demand and cost mechanisms can overlap; broad causation and distribution remain conditional.

deviations.to: Maps the single consequences objective actually evaluated
deviations.why: Borrower/lender evaluation is wholly within inflation consequences; adding another objective would manufacture coverage.
